title: Design WhatsApp: Chat App System Design
summary: An end-to-end system design of a WhatsApp-style chat app: requirements with scale estimates, architecture, WebSocket gateways, message storage, receipts, offline delivery, presence, push, ordering, media and E2EE, closing with scaling, failure handling and interview questions.

chapters.title: Design WhatsApp: Handbook Cover
points: Requirements and scale estimates
High-level architecture
Connection gateway and message flow
Storage, receipts and offline delivery
Presence, push, media and E2EE

chapters.title: Problem, Scope and Requirements
points: Scope in: 1:1 chat, groups up to 1,024 members, media, receipts, presence, push, E2EE; out: calls, status, payments
Scale: 2B users, 500M DAU, 100B messages/day ≈ 1.2M msg/s average, ~3M msg/s peak
Storage: 100B msgs/day × ~100 B ≈ 10 TB/day text; media ~5% of messages at ~200 KB ≈ 1 PB/day, stored briefly
Connections: 500M concurrent WebSockets; at ~200K per server ≈ 2,500+ gateway servers
Latency targets: online delivery p99 < 200 ms; availability 99.99%; no message loss (at-least-once, deduped to exactly-once display)

chapters.title: High-Level Architecture
points: Clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a stateless-logic gateway behind an L4 load balancer
Session service maps user_id → gateway node in Redis; used to route messages to the right gateway
Chat service: validates, assigns ID, persists, then routes or queues for offline
Async backbone: Kafka partitioned by conversation_id for fan-out, push and storage writers
Separate HTTP path for media upload/download via object store and CDN

chapters.title: WebSocket Connection Gateway
points: Responsibility: hold long-lived sockets, authenticate, heartbeat every ~30 s, forward frames to chat service
One server holds ~200K–1M idle connections: tune file descriptors, ~10 KB memory per connection
Connect flow: TLS handshake → auth token → register user_id→gateway in Redis with TTL ~60 s refreshed by heartbeat
APIs: WS frames send, ack, receipt, typing, presence; REST fallback for long-poll on bad networks

Failures: gateway crash drops its sockets, clients reconnect with exponential backoff plus jitter to avoid thundering herd; metrics: connections per node, connect rate, reconnect rate, heartbeat misses

chapters.title: One-to-One Message Flow and Ordering
points: Flow: sender → gateway A → chat service persists → lookup session → gateway B → receiver; server ACK to sender after persist
Client generates a client_msg_id (UUID) so retries are idempotent and deduplicated server-side
Ordering is per conversation only: server assigns monotonic sequence number per conversation_id, no global order
Snowflake-style 64-bit message IDs (timestamp + shard + sequence) are sortable and unique without coordination
Failure: lost ACK triggers client retry with same client_msg_id, server returns the stored result; metrics: send-to-deliver latency p50/p99, duplicate rate

chapters.title: Message Storage
points: Access pattern: write-heavy, append-only, read recent messages by conversation, so use a wide-column store (Cassandra/HBase) over SQL
Table messages: partition key conversation_id, clustering key message_id DESC, columns sender_id, body, type, created_at
Large chats bucket partitions by (conversation_id, month) to avoid hot, unbounded partitions
Inbox table per user holds undelivered messages and is deleted after delivery ACK, so the server is a transit buffer
API: GET /conversations/{id}/messages?before=message_id&limit=50; failure: node loss tolerated with replication factor 3 and quorum writes; metrics: write p99, partition size, disk usage

chapters.title: Delivery and Read Receipts
points: Three states: sent (server stored, one tick), delivered (device received, two ticks), read (user opened, blue ticks)
Receipts are small messages routed back to the sender over the same path, with batched read receipts per conversation up to a last_read_message_id
Data model: per-user last_delivered_id and last_read_id per conversation, not one row per message
Group receipts: aggregate per member, shown as delivered/read only when all members reach it; details in message-info view
Failure: offline sender gets receipts queued in its inbox; metrics: receipt latency p99, receipt share of traffic (~30%)

chapters.title: Group Messaging and Fan-out
points: Group table: group_id, members list (max 1,024), admins; membership cached in Redis
Fan-out on write: store one message copy, then push a delivery task per member via Kafka; a 1,024-member group yields 1,024 deliveries
Server-side fan-out beats client sending N copies: saves mobile bandwidth and keeps one canonical order
Sequence per group gives all members an identical order; member added gets history only from the join point
Failure: partial fan-out is retried per member from Kafka, idempotent by (message_id, member); metrics: fan-out lag, deliveries per message

chapters.title: Offline Delivery and Push Notifications
points: If session lookup misses, message stays in the recipient's inbox queue and a push job is created
Push via APNs (iOS) and FCM (Android) with a small payload, no plaintext under E2EE; the app wakes and fetches
On reconnect the client sends last_seen_message_id and the server drains the inbox in order, then deletes after ACK
Inbox retention ~30 days, then dropped; collapse key merges multiple pushes into one notification
Failure: invalid or expired push token pruned on APNs/FCM error; push provider outage degrades to fetch-on-open; metrics: push success rate, offline-to-delivered latency

chapters.title: Presence and Typing Indicators
points: Presence = online if heartbeat seen within ~60 s; stored in Redis as key with TTL, last_seen written on disconnect
Subscribe model: push presence only to contacts with the chat open, not all contacts, to cut fan-out (500 contacts × status flaps)
Typing indicators are ephemeral: sent through the gateway, never persisted, dropped if recipient offline
Debounce flapping: delay offline status ~5–10 s to ignore brief network drops
Failure: Redis loss only shows stale presence, which is acceptable; metrics: presence update QPS, Redis memory, staleness

chapters.title: Media Sharing and End-to-End Encryption
points: Media flow: client encrypts file with a random key, uploads blob via pre-signed URL to object store, sends URL + key + hash inside the E2EE message
Server stores only ciphertext; thumbnails are generated on the client, CDN caches ciphertext; blobs expire after ~30 days
E2EE uses the Signal protocol: identity key, signed prekey and one-time prekeys uploaded to the server; X3DH sets up a session
Double Ratchet derives a new key per message, giving forward secrecy; groups use sender keys, one encrypt per message
Trade-off: server cannot search or moderate content; multi-device needs per-device keys; metrics: upload success rate, key-fetch latency

chapters.title: Scaling, Failure Handling, Trade-offs and Interview Questions
points: Shard chat service and storage by conversation_id; shard sessions by user_id with consistent hashing; add gateways horizontally
Deploy multi-region: user homed to nearest region, cross-region replication via Kafka; region failover with DNS
Trade-offs: at-least-once plus dedupe vs exactly-once; fan-out on write vs read; WebSocket vs long polling
Interview Q: how do you keep order in a group, and what happens when a gateway dies mid-delivery?
Interview Q: how to handle a celebrity-size group or channel with 1M members (switch to fan-out on read, pull model)

chapters.title: WhatsApp Design Cheatsheet
points: Numbers: 500M concurrent sockets, 1.2M msg/s avg, 10 TB/day text, 200K sockets per gateway
Path: client → gateway → chat service → Kafka → inbox/store → gateway or push
Keys: client_msg_id for idempotency, per-conversation sequence for order, last_read_id for receipts
Stores: Cassandra messages, Redis sessions and presence, S3 plus CDN media, Kafka queues
Pitfalls: global ordering, per-message receipt rows, storing plaintext media, presence broadcast to all contacts
